content: Galaxy Zoo is an online astronomy project that encourages members of the public to participate in the classification of over a million galaxies. The project was inspired by Stardust@home, a NASA initiative that asked the public to search for interstellar dust impacts in images from a comet mission. Galaxy Zoo is a collaborative effort involving Oxford University, Portsmouth University, Johns Hopkins University, and Fingerprint Digital Media in Belfast. Volunteers in the Galaxy Zoo project are tasked with determining whether galaxies in the provided images are elliptical or spiral. If a galaxy is spiral, they are further asked to identify whether it rotates in a clockwise or counterclockwise direction. These images were captured automatically by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey using a digital camera mounted on a telescope at the Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico, USA. The goal of this project is to gather valuable data on the distribution of different types of galaxies, which will help scientists evaluate the accuracy of existing galactic models. Theoretical models suggest that spiral galaxies can merge to form ellipticals, and ellipticals can transform into spirals if they acquire additional gas or stars. Furthermore, Professor Michael Longo from the University of Michigan has proposed that the rotation of spiral galaxies may not be random. If proven correct, this would necessitate a significant revision of current cosmological theories. His claim is based on a survey of 1,660 galaxies, but a larger sample size is needed to confirm or refute this hypothesis. Computer algorithms have proven unreliable in classifying galaxies, which is why human volunteers are essential to the project. According to Kevin Schawinski, a member of the Galaxy Zoo team, the human brain is significantly better than computers at recognizing patterns in these images. Without the help of volunteers, it would take researchers years to analyze the photographs. However, with the participation of 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers, the classification process could be completed in just one month. No prior knowledge of astronomy is required to participate, and volunteers can make initial guesses before being shown the correct answers. Additionally, participants are shown images of stars and satellite trails, which the robotic telescope recorded but could not classify. Volunteers are tested on additional images and allowed to sign up if they achieve a reasonable level of accuracy. Chris Lintott, another member of the Galaxy Zoo team, highlighted one of the unique aspects of the project: participants have the opportunity to view parts of the universe that have never been seen before. The images were captured by a robotic telescope and processed automatically, meaning that the first galaxy a volunteer sees is likely one that no human has ever observed. Kevin Schawinski confirmed this, stating that most of these galaxies have only been seen by robotic systems and computers, making this the first time they are being viewed by human eyes. As of August 2, 2007, Galaxy Zoo announced in its first newsletter that 80,000 volunteers had already classified over 10 million galaxy images, achieving the goals set for the first phase of the project. The project now aims to continue its progress and expand its scope. Galaxy Zoo also features an online forum where volunteers can share and discuss the most striking images they encounter during their classifications. This platform fosters a sense of community and allows participants to engage more deeply with the project.
